title: Weather Rescue Brazil: nineteenth-century weather observations transcribed by a small offline model
description:
Daily, dekadal and monthly meteorological observations from six stations, 1851-1890, transcribed from printed nineteenth-century tables: the Annales de l'Observatoire Impérial de Rio de Janeiro (French), the Revista do Observatório (Portuguese) and the Astronomical and Meteorological Observations made at the Radcliffe Observatory, Oxford (English).

7,418 rows, 3,999 usable, 48,355 values, 259 pages. Variables include barometric pressure read seven times daily, temperature maxima, minima and means, relative humidity, vapour tension, cloudiness, wind direction and force, rainfall, evaporation, ozone and actinometry.

Transcription is by a Qwen3.5-2B model with a LoRA adapter running offline on a laptop. Each printed layout is described by a JSON profile declaring its columns, units, physical ranges and the arithmetic the page asserts about itself, which is used to judge every row without a human. Fifteen of the eighteen layouts needed no labelled rows at all. Total API spend across the project was US$1.56.

External validation. Oxford has published the same observations the Radcliffe tables hold, digitised independently more than a century later. Of the cells this dataset calls usable, 100% of the dry bulb (252 cells) and 96.7% of the rainfall (300 cells) agree with that series; of the rainfall cells it flags, 44.4% do. The quality verdict predicts agreement with an independent source, which is the part of this work that is hardest to obtain and easiest to check.

Read the dataset card before using it. What checks_pass verifies differs by publication, and it is not a uniform quality tier. No row has been verified line-by-line by a human; the 3,822-cell evaluation gold set has been, and is separate from the dataset.

Images: Biblioteca Digital de Obras Raras do Observatório Nacional, via DocVirt, and the Internet Archive. The observations themselves are public domain (Lei 9.610) and are not ours to licence. The transcriptions, verdicts and provenance are dedicated to the public domain under CC0; the pipeline code and model weights are Apache-2.0.
